paragraphs: Sensory information arrives continuously and can contain different numbers of informative dimensions. This paper asks how a neural network could adjust the dimensionality of its representation as that information changes. It extends an earlier similarity-matching approach whose output dimensionality was fixed in advance by the number of output neurons.

The authors formulate three optimization objectives that connect this adaptation to the input covariance matrix: a description of how input variations occur together. In the offline setting, their solutions project data onto its principal subspace. The three objectives treat the associated eigenvalues differently, using soft thresholding, hard thresholding, or thresholding followed by equalization to determine the output representation.

The paper then derives corresponding algorithms for processing data online and expresses them as neuronal activity with biologically plausible local learning rules. In two of the resulting networks, neurons separate into classes identified with principal neurons and interneurons. The contribution is an objective-based account of adaptive dimensionality reduction that also yields plausible neural implementations.
neurips-2015-a-normative-theory-of-adapt.tldr: Three optimization objectives yield biologically plausible neural algorithms that adapt output dimensionality to the statistical structure of incoming data.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks to recover independent source signals from observations that mix them linearly. Gaussian noise complicates both learning how the signals were mixed and separating them effectively. This paper addresses these two tasks together, while distinguishing recovery of the mixing model from recovery of the underlying signals.

The proposed algorithm, PEGI, uses a fixed-point iteration in a pseudo-Euclidean space, where the inner-product-like operation is indefinite. This geometric choice resolves technical difficulties shared by several existing noisy ICA algorithms. The authors provide provable model recovery and report that the method is efficient and accurate in testing.

The second contribution concerns signal quality. Simply applying the inverse mixing matrix can be suboptimal under the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio criterion. The authors show how any solution to mixing-matrix reconstruction can instead produce an SINR-optimal demixing, even though SINR cannot itself be computed from the observed data. Combining this result with PEGI yields a practical recovery method with an optimality guarantee for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise.
neurips-2015-a-pseudo-euclidean-iteratio.tldr: PEGI combines a new geometric iteration for noisy ICA with a construction that makes reconstructed mixing models yield SINR-optimal signal recovery.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a polynomial by choosing inputs and observing its values. Although an n-variable polynomial on binary inputs has exponentially many possible monomials, only s coefficients are nonzero. The authors exploit this sparsity through sampling strategies inspired by sparse-graph error-correcting codes, connecting query design in learning with coding theory.

The recovery guarantee uses an ensemble-average assumption: the polynomial is drawn uniformly from an ensemble with specified size and sparsity. For sparsity up to O(2^(δn)), with any δ between zero and one, the framework learns the polynomial exactly with high probability using O(ns) queries and O(ns log s) time. The stated result also accommodates Gaussian perturbations of the queries.

The authors additionally express graph cuts as polynomial evaluations to infer an unknown sparse graph. Exploiting graph structure gives a cut-query requirement described as almost linear in the number of edges and sublinear in the number of nodes. Experiments on real datasets report substantial runtime and query savings over competitive methods.
neurips-2015-an-active-learning-framewor.tldr: Coding-inspired query strategies efficiently recover sparse polynomials under an ensemble assumption and extend to learning graphs from cut queries.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether sparse principal components can be recovered from a sketch containing only a small selection of a data matrix's entries. Its approach connects incomplete data to optimization accuracy: instead of requiring the full matrix, it studies when a smaller representation preserves enough information to obtain a nearly optimal answer.

The central result applies to a broad class of optimization problems. If the sketch approximates the original matrix closely in spectral norm, optimizing with the sketch can yield a near-optimal solution. For sparse PCA on m observations with n dimensions, the authors obtain an ε-additive approximation using O(ε^(-2) k̃ max{m,n}) entries, where k̃ is the matrix's stable rank.

The experiments cover image, text, biological, and financial data. They demonstrate recovery of sparse principal components from incomplete data and report runtime reductions of at least a factor of five using the sparse sketch. The findings connect a conditional approximation guarantee with a practical computational benefit: fewer retained entries can support useful sparse PCA solutions while reducing processing time.
neurips-2015-approximating-sparse-pca-fr.tldr: Spectrally accurate sketches support provably approximate sparse PCA from relatively few matrix entries and substantially reduce runtime in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: BACKSHIFT learns linear causal models that can contain feedback cycles and latent variables. It uses equilibrium observations collected under shift interventions. A central feature is that the intervention locations and strengths need not be supplied beforehand; the method can estimate them from the data alongside the causal system.

The computation uses only second moments, specifically differences between covariance matrices from different experimental settings. BACKSHIFT applies joint matrix diagonalization to those differences. This makes variation between settings the basis for identifying the causal relationships, while keeping the method centered on comparatively simple matrix operations.

The authors establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability, meaning that the system can be uniquely distinguished from the available information. Under the stated general assumptions, this condition holds almost surely if and only if at least three distinct experimental settings are available; one may be purely observational. They demonstrate the method on simulations, flow cytometry, and financial time series. Its scope therefore combines feedback and hidden variables with a specific intervention and equilibrium-data setting.
neurips-2015-backshift-learning-causal-c.tldr: BACKSHIFT uses covariance differences across intervention settings to identify linear cyclic causal systems without knowing intervention locations or strengths.

paragraphs: The paper studies a stochastic version of normalized gradient descent, which updates using gradient direction rather than the full gradient magnitude. Its aim is to extend efficient optimization guarantees beyond the familiar setting of convex functions with a global Lipschitz condition. Normalizing the gradient changes what information determines an optimization step.

The authors prove convergence to a global minimum for functions that are quasi-convex and locally Lipschitz. Quasi-convexity extends the idea of unimodality to several dimensions and permits certain saddle points. The local Lipschitz requirement only applies in a small region around the optimum, allowing the analysis to avoid demanding the same control throughout the entire domain.

These assumptions address difficulties associated with saddle points and exploding gradients while retaining a global convergence result for the specified function class. The analysis also reveals a requirement that differs from vanilla stochastic gradient descent: stochastic normalized gradient descent provably needs a minimum minibatch size. The result therefore links the broader optimization guarantee to sufficient averaging of stochastic gradient information, rather than treating normalization alone as adequate.
neurips-2015-beyond-convexity-stochastic.tldr: Stochastic normalized gradient descent has a global convergence guarantee for quasi-convex, locally Lipschitz functions, but requires a minimum minibatch size.

paragraphs: Multilabel prediction assigns several possible labels to an instance, and different evaluation metrics can favor different prediction rules. This paper builds a framework for analyzing those metrics and characterizing classifiers that are optimal for the underlying population. It also clarifies how relationships between labels enter the optimal decision.

For the instance-, micro-, and macro-averaged metrics covered by the analysis, the population-optimal classifier decomposes into binary decisions based on each label's conditional marginal distribution. The labels retain a weak association through the decision threshold. Thus, the framework explains how per-label probability information can support a joint evaluation objective without requiring all label relationships to enter each binary decision directly.

Using this characterization, the authors propose a computationally efficient, general-purpose plug-in classifier and prove consistency for the metric being optimized. This extends analysis beyond a few previously understood metrics, including Hamming loss, to many commonly used measures. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets support the theory, connecting the population-level characterization to a practical classification procedure.
neurips-2015-consistent-multilabel-class.tldr: A framework for multilabel metrics yields population-optimal threshold rules and an efficient plug-in classifier with consistency guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper develops deep generative models for sequences, with the goal of learning how observations depend on earlier parts of a time series. Its architecture builds a hierarchy of temporal sigmoid belief networks. Each temporal network is itself a sequence of sigmoid belief networks, giving the model both temporal organization and multiple layers.

Information from preceding networks enters through a contextual hidden state that regulates the current network's hidden bias. This provides a mechanism for past context to influence the model's present behavior. To make learning and inference scalable, the authors introduce a recognition model that quickly samples from an approximate, variational posterior. It is trained jointly with the generative model by maximizing a lower bound on log-likelihood.

The experiments span bouncing balls, polyphonic music, motion capture, and text streams. The authors report state-of-the-art predictive performance on these evaluations and show that the model can synthesize different sequences. The contribution combines a temporal generative architecture with an inference mechanism intended to make that architecture practical to train.
neurips-2015-deep-temporal-sigmoid-belie.tldr: Hierarchies of temporal sigmoid belief networks combine contextual sequence modeling with fast variational inference for prediction and synthesis.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is widely used for collaborative filtering, but an online recommender also has to decide what to learn about next. This becomes especially important during cold start, when recommendations must balance current estimates of relevance with opportunities to gather information about new or rarely recommended items.

The paper introduces Particle Thompson Sampling for Matrix-Factorization to combine those two aims automatically. It uses the Thompson sampling framework together with an efficient online Bayesian matrix-factorization method. A Rao-Blackwellized particle filter provides the probabilistic machinery for updating the model as recommendation feedback arrives, bringing uncertainty-aware decision making into the matrix-factorization setting.

This matters because choosing an item can both serve the user now and inform future recommendations. The algorithm treats that exploration–exploitation tradeoff as part of recommendation itself. Experiments on several real-world collaborative-filtering datasets report significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The stated findings support the combination of online Bayesian updates and Thompson sampling as an effective approach in those evaluations.
neurips-2015-efficient-thompson-sampling.tldr: Particle Thompson Sampling combines online Bayesian matrix factorization with exploration to improve recommendations on several real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a neural network that repeatedly directs attention over an external memory, which may be large. The model can perform several computational steps, called hops, before producing each output symbol. These repeated memory-access steps are a central architectural feature rather than a single lookup attached to an otherwise unchanged prediction process.

The network is trained end to end. Compared with the earlier Memory Network described in the abstract, this substantially reduces the supervision required during training. That reduction matters for applicability: the architecture can be trained with less instructional information while retaining the ability to make multiple passes over its memory.

The authors evaluate the model on synthetic question answering and language modeling. For question answering, it is competitive with Memory Networks while using less supervision. On Penn TreeBank and Text8, its language-modeling performance is comparable to recurrent neural networks and LSTMs. In both task categories, multiple hops improve results. The findings support repeated attention-based computation as a useful component across these distinct applications.
neurips-2015-end-to-end-memory-networks-.tldr: End-to-end Memory Networks repeatedly attend to external memory, reducing supervision needs and improving results through multiple computational hops.

paragraphs: Mixture models combine simpler models with weights to represent richer distributions. Expectation maximization offers convenient updates for many such models, but their nonconvex likelihoods leave it without known global convergence guarantees. Moment-based methods provide global guarantees for some mixtures, yet deriving them across many model families has been difficult.

Polymom offers a unifying moment-based framework for models whose individual components have moments that are polynomial functions of their parameters. The key observation is that the full mixture's moments are weighted combinations of those same polynomials. This lets the authors express parameter estimation as a Generalized Moment Problem rather than deriving a separate procedure from scratch for each model.

The framework solves relaxations of that problem with semidefinite optimization and extracts parameters using ideas from computer algebra. Its contribution is a common route from a model's polynomial moments to an estimation procedure, linking statistical estimation with convex optimization and algebraic tools. Simulations show good empirical performance on several models; the stated applicability condition is the polynomial form of component moments.
neurips-2015-estimating-mixture-models-v.tldr: Polymom turns mixture estimation with polynomial component moments into a common framework using semidefinite optimization and algebraic parameter extraction.

paragraphs: The paper studies distributed algorithms for k-center clustering, including a version that accommodates outliers in noisy data. Its motivation is the growing scale of datasets, which makes distributing computation attractive. The central question is whether this distribution can preserve strong clustering quality while providing practical speed and memory benefits.

For the noise-free problem, the authors prove that a previously proposed distributed method has a constant-factor approximation guarantee. This supplies a theoretical explanation for its observed empirical strength. For the setting with outliers, they develop a new distributed algorithm with another constant-factor guarantee. Both algorithms are highly parallel and designed to fit a broad range of distributed computing frameworks.

Empirical comparisons with leading noisy sequential clustering methods show that the distributed algorithms remain consistently close to their sequential versions. The authors also describe them as fast and memory efficient. Together, the results support distributed clustering through two forms of evidence: bounded approximation quality in the analysis and close agreement with sequential counterparts in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2015-fast-distributed-k-center-c.tldr: Distributed k-center algorithms achieve constant-factor approximation guarantees, including with outliers, and empirically stay close to sequential counterparts.

paragraphs: This paper examines the ongoing cost of maintaining machine-learning systems after their initial predictive capability has been built. It uses technical debt as its organizing idea: rapid development can create obligations that become expensive to manage later. The authors argue that substantial maintenance burdens are common in real-world ML systems despite the speed of early progress.

Their analysis identifies risks involving system boundaries, tightly entangled components, hidden feedback loops, and consumers whose dependencies have not been declared. These categories draw attention to how a predictive system connects to the rest of its environment. The maintenance concern extends beyond the model to relationships among data, software, and the systems that use its outputs.

Other risk factors include data dependencies, configuration problems, external-world changes, and recurring system-level anti-patterns. The paper's contribution is a design-oriented account of these ML-specific sources of debt. Its message is that judging a system by how quickly it becomes useful leaves out the continuing work required to maintain that usefulness as its surrounding dependencies and conditions evolve.
neurips-2015-hidden-technical-debt-in-ma.tldr: Machine-learning systems can accumulate substantial maintenance debt through data dependencies, entanglement, feedback loops, configuration, and changes around them.

paragraphs: Simple decision heuristics describe behavior using only a little information and straightforward ways of combining it. A decision might rely on one cue, examine cues in sequence, or assign them equal weight. This paper asks how quickly such rules can be learned from experience, separating the simplicity of using a rule from the question of learning it.

The authors study three families: single-cue decisions, lexicographic decisions, and tallying. These correspond to relying on one piece of information, considering information in an ordered sequence, and combining it with equal weighting. The analysis therefore covers several different forms of simple decision making rather than treating all heuristics as one interchangeable approach.

Both theoretical analysis and empirical results show that a few training samples can produce substantial learning progress. The empirical study uses 63 natural datasets spanning diverse subjects. The finding concerns meaningful early improvement, rather than a claim that a handful of examples completes learning. It helps explain how simple behavioral rules can become useful even when experience is limited.
neurips-2015-learning-from-small-samples.tldr: Analytical results and experiments across 63 datasets show substantial early learning progress for three families of simple decision heuristics.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires producing outputs with internal organization, rather than only a single recognition decision. This paper addresses the difficulty of representing such outputs probabilistically with conventional supervised deep networks. It develops a conditional generative model in which Gaussian latent variables support stochastic predictions conditioned on the input.

The model is trained using stochastic gradient variational Bayes and predicts through fast stochastic feed-forward inference. This combination provides a way to learn a structured output representation and generate different outputs from it. The authors also introduce recurrent prediction networks, noise injection into inputs, and training with predictions at multiple scales as strategies for improving robustness.

Experiments show that the proposed model can generate diverse yet realistic outputs compared with deterministic deep-network counterparts. The architectural and training strategies provide complementary benefits, leading to strong pixel-level object segmentation and semantic labeling results on Caltech-UCSD Birds 200 and a subset of Labeled Faces in the Wild. The findings connect probabilistic output generation with practical structured-prediction performance in these evaluations.
neurips-2015-learning-structured-output-.tldr: A deep conditional generative model uses Gaussian latent variables and stochastic inference to produce diverse structured outputs with strong reported segmentation performance.

paragraphs: Human vision recognizes concepts under difficult conditions, but it also brings biases to recognition. This paper investigates whether some of those biases can be estimated and transferred into machine vision. The aim is to capture useful tendencies in human recognition in a form that a computer classifier can incorporate.

The authors introduce a method inspired by tools from human psychophysics that estimates possible human visual biases directly in computer-vision feature spaces. Their experiments suggest that classifiers associated with human vision can be transferred to machines with some success. This provides the basis for incorporating those biases into a learned recognition rule.

They then formulate a support vector machine whose separating hyperplane is constrained to have an orientation consistent with the estimated human bias. This makes the bias an explicit influence on the classifier's decision boundary. The reported results suggest that such transfer may improve generalization across datasets and recognition with very little training data. These are encouraging empirical findings, expressed as possible benefits rather than universal guarantees.
neurips-2015-learning-visual-biases-from.tldr: Estimated human visual biases can guide an SVM's decision boundary and may improve recognition across datasets and with little training data.

paragraphs: Lifelong learning studies how experience across tasks can help with learning additional tasks. Earlier theoretical analyses often assumed tasks were sampled independently from a fixed environment, or imposed strong restrictions on data distributions. This paper extends the foundations to two settings where the observed tasks are not an independent, identically distributed sample.

In the first setting, tasks still come from the same environment but may depend on one another. The authors prove a PAC-Bayesian theorem that directly generalizes an earlier result for independent tasks. This separates the assumption of a common task environment from the stronger requirement that every sampled task be independent of the others.

In the second setting, the task environment itself can change over time. The authors propose learning an inductive bias represented as a transfer procedure, provide a generalization bound, and use a toy example to show how the bound can identify a beneficial transfer algorithm. The contribution supplies theoretical routes for learning across dependent tasks and changing environments within the analyzed scenarios.
neurips-2015-lifelong-learning-with-non-.tldr: The paper extends lifelong-learning theory to dependent tasks and changing task environments through generalization bounds and learned transfer procedures.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an idealized problem in which a learner repeatedly divides several types of resources among multiple tasks. Giving a task more resources increases its chance of completion. The learner must make these decisions without knowing how well each resource type aligns with each task, and the resulting feedback is noisy.

The main contribution is both this learning setting and an algorithm with a nearly optimal regret analysis. Regret measures the cost of decisions made while the learner is still discovering how to allocate resources effectively. The guarantee therefore addresses the cumulative consequences of learning through allocation, rather than only the quality of a final allocation.

The analysis connects the problem to stochastic linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise, meaning that observation noise need not have uniform variance. The authors also obtain new results for stochastic linear bandits on the hypercube, reporting substantial improvements over existing work, especially in sparse cases. These connections make the contribution relevant both to the resource-allocation formulation and to the associated bandit problems.
neurips-2015-linear-multi-resource-alloc.tldr: A sequential multi-resource allocation model yields a nearly regret-optimal algorithm and improved results for related stochastic linear bandit problems.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which samples to collect based on what would be most informative for the learner. This makes evaluation different from applying several algorithms to one fixed benchmark: each algorithm's choices help determine the data it receives. Real-world comparison therefore requires an adaptive data-collection process as part of the experiment.

NEXT is an open-source system built to support that process at large scale. It provides a platform for developing, testing, and deploying active-learning methods in real applications, with reproducible research as a central purpose. The paper describes the challenges involved in building this infrastructure and demonstrates its capabilities through several experiments.

The experimental results show that testing active-learning algorithms in this way can expose strengths and weaknesses that are sometimes unexpected. The contribution is therefore a research and application platform that makes adaptive experimentation possible, alongside evidence of what such experimentation can reveal. It supports evaluating algorithms through the data-collection behavior that defines active learning, rather than treating sample selection as separate from evaluation.
neurips-2015-next-a-system-for-real-worl.tldr: NEXT provides open-source infrastructure for reproducible active-learning experiments in which algorithms adaptively collect their own data.

paragraphs: Classifier chains model dependencies among the labels assigned to one instance by arranging label predictions in an ordered chain. Their performance can depend strongly on that ordering. This paper addresses how to select the order systematically, rather than leaving a consequential modeling choice unspecified or treating all orders as equivalent.

The authors first generalize the classifier-chain model to allow a random label order and analyze its generalization error. That theoretical treatment motivates two search algorithms. CC-DP uses dynamic programming to search for a globally optimal label order for the chain, while CC-Greedy seeks a locally optimal classifier chain.

Experiments on real-world multilabel datasets from several domains show CC-DP outperforming the compared state-of-the-art approaches. CC-Greedy achieves prediction performance comparable to CC-DP in those evaluations. The results give label ordering both a theoretical treatment and practical algorithms, while distinguishing the global and local search objectives. The empirical similarity of the two methods concerns predictive performance; it does not make their optimization guarantees identical.
neurips-2015-on-the-optimality-of-classi.tldr: A theoretical analysis of classifier-chain ordering motivates globally optimal dynamic-programming search and a greedy alternative with comparable reported prediction performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions where choosing an action also supplies information about other actions' payoffs. Every observation is Gaussian with the corresponding action's mean payoff, but its variance depends on both the chosen action and the action being observed. Variance may be infinite, allowing the model to represent missing useful information.

This setup describes information transfer more finely than feedback models that only specify which actions reveal which others. Two observations about the same action can have different usefulness because they have different variances. The authors derive problem-dependent lower bounds on regret that apply at finite time to every algorithm, while recovering known asymptotic and finite-time minimax bounds.

They also provide algorithms approaching these limits: one achieves the problem-dependent lower bound within a universal constant factor, while another reaches minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. The contribution pairs a richer model of side observations with guarantees about both unavoidable learning cost and achievable performance, making observation quality part of the theoretical account.
neurips-2015-online-learning-with-gaussi.tldr: A Gaussian side-observation model captures varying information quality and admits finite-time regret lower bounds with algorithms that nearly match them.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate an unknown matrix in trace regression, a setting relevant to matrix completion, quantum state tomography, and compressed sensing. Popular approaches use regularization to encourage a low-rank estimate. Nuclear norm regularization is one such approach, adding a preference for low rank to the estimation procedure.

The authors argue that this extra regularization may be unnecessary when the unknown matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite and the measurement design satisfies certain conditions. They consider least squares estimation constrained to matrices with that structure. The central idea is that this structural constraint, together with suitable design conditions, may suffice to obtain performance comparable to regularized estimation.

The comparison is with regularization methods whose tuning parameter has been properly chosen. Choosing that parameter entails knowledge of the noise level and/or tuning, whereas the constrained least squares approach has no tuning parameter. Its appeal is therefore practical simplicity with potentially comparable performance under the stated conditions. The claim remains conditional on the matrix structure and design; it does not establish that regularization is unnecessary throughout trace regression.
neurips-2015-regularization-free-estimat.tldr: Under suitable design conditions, least squares constrained to symmetric positive semidefinite matrices may match properly tuned regularized methods without a tuning parameter.

paragraphs: Expectation maximization is widely used for models with latent variables, but high-dimensional problems can make its maximization step ill-defined. This paper develops a unified regularized EM framework for that setting. The aim is to make the iterative procedure workable while providing statistical guarantees about the estimates it produces.

Regularization must serve two purposes during EM: support progress toward a solution and identify useful structure, such as sparsity or low rank. The authors emphasize that directly applying standard high-dimensional regularization prescriptions to each maximization step does not guarantee the right balance. Their algorithm and analysis are developed together to expose the relationship between optimization error and statistical error.

The framework is specialized to sparse Gaussian mixtures, high-dimensional mixed regression, and regression with missing variables, yielding statistical guarantees for each example. This gives a common treatment of several latent-variable estimation problems. The contribution concerns how regularization interacts with the sequence of EM updates, making the iterative learning process itself part of the statistical analysis.
neurips-2015-regularized-em-algorithms-a.tldr: A unified regularized EM framework balances iterative optimization with structural estimation and provides guarantees for several high-dimensional latent-variable models.

paragraphs: Deploying deep-learning systems on mobile devices requires managing limited storage and power. This paper proposes learning structured parameter matrices to make those systems more compact and computationally efficient. The matrices belong to a broad family characterized by low displacement rank, which provides a unified way to describe different parameter-sharing arrangements.

The framework allows modeling capacity to be tuned along a continuum from strongly structured matrices toward unstructured ones. Its transforms also support fast function and gradient evaluation, so the intended computational benefit applies both when making predictions and during training. This connects compact parameterization with the cost of forward and backward computation.

Experiments report improved tradeoffs among accuracy, compactness, and speed compared with several existing techniques. In mobile speech keyword spotting, the proposed methods are much more effective than standard linear low-rank bottleneck layers. They achieve more than 3.5-fold compression while nearly retaining state-of-the-art model performance. The results support structured transforms as a practical way to reduce model size without sacrificing comparable amounts of predictive quality.
neurips-2015-structured-transforms-for-s.tldr: Learnable structured matrices improve accuracy–size–speed tradeoffs and achieve over 3.5-fold compression with nearly retained performance in mobile keyword spotting.

paragraphs: This paper presents one algorithmic framework for recovering planted solutions in stochastic block models and planted constraint satisfaction problems. It relates both settings to random bipartite graphs, allowing a shared recovery method and analysis. The algorithm uses power iteration with subsampling and runs in time linear in the number of edges it processes.

Its edge or constraint requirement for perfect recovery matches the best-known bounds within a constant factor. The authors report substantially better time complexity than spectral and semidefinite-programming approaches. Their main advance concerns bipartite graphs with unequal partition sizes, which arise in the reduction from planted constraint problems: the algorithm succeeds at substantially lower density than spectral methods.

That recovery result passes a barrier associated with the spectral norm of a random matrix. Analyzing the subsampled iterations requires tracking multiple norms of the evolving solution. The algorithm can also be implemented with very limited access to the input distribution. Its simple implementation and linear runtime make the proposed framework suitable for very large instances within the studied models.
neurips-2015-subsampled-power-iteration-.tldr: Subsampled power iteration recovers planted structures in linear time and improves the recovery density over spectral approaches for unequal bipartitions.
